Babylonians
bab-ih-LOH-nee-uns
n. pl.
The people of Babylon, Hebrew Babel, confusion — the city of Genesis 11 and the empire of Nebuchadnezzar. Ezekiel calls them the Babylonians of Chaldea, the land of their nativity. From Genesis to Revelation, Babylon is Scripture’s standing name for the city of man set against the city of God.

Biblical Definition

The Babylonians are the Chaldean empire that took Jerusalem, burned the temple, and carried Judah into the seventy years. God names them as His own instrument in language even more startling than He uses of Assyria: I will send and take all the families of the north… and Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant (Jeremiah 25:9). Habakkuk could not stomach it and said so in the great prophetic complaint, and God’s answer begins, lo, I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation (Habakkuk 1:6). Daniel opens with the fact stated flatly and with the theology in the next verse — the Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand. Ezekiel uses them in his most searing indictment of Judah’s political adultery: the Babylonians came to her into the bed of love (Ezekiel 23:17), the alliance Judah courted becoming the power that destroyed her. And to the exiles already in that city Jeremiah wrote the letter that has governed Christian civic life ever since: build houses, plant gardens, take wives, and seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives (Jeremiah 29:7). Revelation ends the account: Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines BABYLONIAN as pertaining to Babylon, and BABYLONISH as pertaining to Babylon, or, figuratively, mixed and confused — a sense taken from the confusion of tongues at Babel and carried into Reformation polemic against Rome.

expand to see more

BABYLONIAN, a. — Pertaining to Babylon, the ancient city on the Euphrates, or to the empire of which it was the capital.

BABYLONIAN, n. — An inhabitant of Babylonia; also, in the older writers, an astrologer, from the reputation of the Chaldean star-gazers.

BABYLONISH, a. — Pertaining to Babylon; also mixed, confused — from the confusion of tongues at Babel (Genesis 11:9).

A goodly Babylonish garment was part of Achan’s spoil at Jericho (Joshua 7:21), the first plunder to destroy an Israelite household.

Webster’s second sense records the Reformation habit, following Revelation 17-18, of calling any corrupt religious system a Babylon.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 25:9 — "Behold, I will send and take all the families of the north, saith the LORD, and Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and will bring them against this land, and against the inhabitants thereof, and against all these nations round about, and will utterly destroy them, and make them an astonishment, and an hissing, and perpetual desolations."

Habakkuk 1:6 — "For, lo, I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation, which shall march through the breadth of the land, to possess the dwellingplaces that are not theirs."

Ezekiel 23:17 — "And the Babylonians came to her into the bed of love, and they defiled her with their whoredom, and she was polluted with them, and her mind was alienated from them."

Jeremiah 29:7 — "And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace."

Revelation 18:2 — "And he cried mightily with a strong voice, saying, Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, and is become the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit, and a cage of every unclean and hateful bird."

Modern Corruption

Jeremiah 29 is quarried for a single verse about God’s plans while the letter it belongs to — a command to settle down under a pagan tyranny for seventy years and pray for its welfare — is passed over entirely.

expand to see more

For I know the thoughts that I think toward you is printed on graduation cards and coffee mugs as a promise of personal prosperity. It was written to a deported people, four verses after they were told to build houses and plant gardens in the land of their captors, and the thoughts of peace God knew toward them were to be realized after seventy years be accomplished at Babylon — that is, after nearly everyone reading the letter was dead. Jeremiah had to add a warning against the prophets among them who were promising a quick return, because that is always the more popular message. The verse is a real promise; it is a promise to a covenant people about a corporate future beyond the lifetime of most who received it, and lifting it out of that is not encouragement but flattery.

The letter’s actual instruction is the more valuable thing, and it is the charter of Christian citizenship under a government that is not Christian. Seek the peace of the city; pray for it; in its peace you shall have peace. That is written of Babylon, the city that had just burned the temple, and it is the same instinct as Paul’s command to pray for kings and all in authority under Nero. It rules out both the withdrawal that treats the surrounding city as no concern of ours and the revolutionary impulse that treats it as the enemy to be overthrown. Daniel served in that administration at the highest level and would not eat the king’s meat or stop praying at his window. That is the pattern: full civic engagement, absolute religious refusal.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Babel (H894), Babylon, connected in Genesis 11:9 with balal, to confound; Kasdim (H3778) is the Chaldeans; Greek Babylon (G897).

expand to see more

Hebrew Babel (H894) — Babel, Babylon; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth (Genesis 11:9).

Hebrew balal (H1101) — to mix, to confound; the wordplay behind the name.

Hebrew Kasdim (H3778) — Chaldeans; the ruling stock of the Babylonian empire (Habakkuk 1:6).

Hebrew Nebukadretstsar (H5019) — Nebuchadnezzar, also spelled Nebuchadrezzar; called my servant at Jeremiah 25:9.

Greek Babylon (G897) — Babylon; the great harlot city of Revelation 17-18 and, most take it, Peter’s cipher in 1 Peter 5:13.

Usage

"Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant (Jeremiah 25:9) — a pagan tyrant given the covenant title of servant."

"Seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away (Jeremiah 29:7) — the charter of exile citizenship."

"Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen (Revelation 18:2) — the end of the city of man."
